faq.q: Build a custom model or buy off-the-shelf?
faq.a: Buy when a general model solves it, build when your data or domain is the edge. We benchmark both, then recommend the cheaper path to your accuracy target. No dogma.

faq.q: How do you stop hallucinations?
faq.a: The assistant answers only from your own sources and quotes them, so every answer can be checked. On top of that sit limits on what it is allowed to say, and an automated accuracy test on every release. We measure how often it makes something up and block the release when that number moves the wrong way. Trust comes from tests, not hope.

faq.q: Do we keep the IP and models?
faq.a: Yes. You own the code, weights, and pipelines outright. No lock-in, no rent on your own models. We hand over everything and document it so your team can run it.

faq.q: How do you keep models accurate after launch?
faq.a: MLOps with monitoring, drift alerts, and eval suites in CI. When quality slips, we retrain or tune fast. Accuracy is a system we maintain, not a launch-day snapshot.

faq.q: We don't think we have enough data. Is ML off the table?
faq.a: Usually not. Pretrained models, fine-tuning and augmentation lower the bar, and a feasibility study tells you in two weeks what your data actually supports. Sometimes the answer is to start collecting the right data now, and we will say exactly that.

faq.q: How do you measure success?
faq.a: Before we train anything, we agree on the metric, the baseline to beat and the threshold that makes production worthwhile. Every demo reports against that harness. If the numbers are not there, you find out in weeks, not after a year of budget.

custom-models.label: Machine Learning
custom-models.title: Custom model development
custom-models.subtitle: Bespoke models trained on your data, delivered as running systems with pipelines, evals and documentation. You own everything.
overview: Off-the-shelf models solve generic problems. When your edge is your data, a pricing history no competitor has, a defect archive from your own line, a decade of claims, a custom model turns that edge into software. We build these models end to end: problem framing, data work, training, evaluation and deployment in one engagement.

The engagement starts with a baseline in the first days, because a simple model that works beats a complex one that might. From there, every increment of complexity has to pay for itself on the evaluation set. You see the metrics weekly, on your data, and you can stop at any point with something that already works.

What changes for you: instead of a notebook and a promise, you get a versioned training pipeline, a deployed model behind an API and the documentation to retrain without us. Weights, code and data pipelines are yours outright, and the handover includes working sessions with the engineers who will own the system.

faq.q: How much data do we need to train a custom model?
faq.a: Less than you think for fine-tuning, more than you hope for training from scratch. A two-week feasibility study on your actual data replaces guessing: you get a baseline score and a clear read on whether more data would move it.

faq.q: Custom model or a fine-tuned foundation model?
faq.a: Fine-tuning wins when a pretrained model already roughly understands your domain; training from scratch wins on narrow, structured problems with plenty of labeled data. We benchmark both against your metric and recommend the cheaper path.

faq.q: What does it cost to run after handover?
faq.a: We size the model for your traffic and budget before training, and the metrics report includes cost per thousand predictions. Most custom models run on modest infrastructure, and the runbook covers scaling up and down.

nlp-llm.title: NLP & LLM engineering
nlp-llm.subtitle: Assistants that answer from your own documents, data extraction, chat and automation, built so quality is measured before anything reaches users.
overview: Most language-model demos take a weekend. Making one reliable enough to face customers or auditors is the real work: making sure every answer comes from your own sources rather than the model's imagination, handling the documents that break parsers, and proving quality release after release. We build assistants, retrieval pipelines (the pattern usually called RAG), extraction services, chat and automation with that bar in mind from day one.

Delivery is evaluation-first. Before we tune prompts or choose a model, we build a test set from your real documents and questions, with pass criteria you agree to. Every change is scored against it, so hallucination rate, extraction accuracy and latency are numbers on a dashboard, not impressions from a demo.

You end up with a system your team can change safely: swap the model when a better one ships, edit prompts, extend the corpus, and the eval suite tells you within minutes whether quality held. Costs are tracked per query, so the decision to scale comes with a price tag attached, not a surprise invoice at month end.

benefits.title: Grounded answers

benefits.title: Evaluation before launch

benefits.title: Structured output you can build on

faq.q: Which model will you use?
faq.a: The one that passes your eval set at the lowest cost. We benchmark OpenAI, Anthropic and open-weight models on your actual tasks, and the architecture keeps the choice reversible.

faq.q: How do you handle confidential documents?

faq.q: What about hallucinations in front of customers?
faq.a: Answers are drawn from your content rather than the model's memory, citations make them checkable, and a limit layer catches output that breaks your rules. We measure how often the system makes something up on a fixed test set and gate releases on that number.

computer-vision.title: Computer vision
computer-vision.subtitle: Detection, OCR and quality inspection trained on your images, tested in your lighting, deployed on your line or in your cloud.
overview: Vision models fail in the gap between the demo dataset and your factory floor: glare, dust, camera angles, the defect that shows up twice a month. We build detection, OCR and quality-inspection systems around that gap, training on your images and evaluating on the hard cases your team collects, not on benchmark photos.

The engagement starts with your existing footage, or a capture plan if there is none. We label a first dataset, train a baseline and show you precision and recall per defect class within weeks. From there the loop is tight: review the misses together, relabel, retrain, until the numbers clear the bar you set.

Deployment fits your constraints: edge devices next to the camera when latency or connectivity demands it, cloud when it does not. The system ships with a review UI for borderline cases, so operators correct the model and every correction becomes training data for the next iteration. Retraining on that growing set is a scheduled pipeline, not a new project.

faq.q: How many images do we need to start?
faq.a: With modern pretrained backbones, a few hundred per class is often enough for a first baseline, and augmentation stretches small sets further. The feasibility study answers it precisely: we train on what you have and report where more data would pay off.

faq.q: Rare defects appear a few times a month. Can a model learn them?
faq.a: Yes, with the right approach: augmentation, synthetic examples and anomaly detection that flags anything unusual rather than only known classes. Recall on rare cases is reported separately, so the risk stays visible.

faq.q: Does this run without internet on the shop floor?
faq.a: Yes. Models export to ONNX and run on industrial PCs or edge devices next to the camera, with updates shipped on your schedule and no cloud dependency at inference time.

forecasting.label: Machine Learning
forecasting.title: Forecasting & time series
forecasting.subtitle: Demand, risk and capacity forecasts that beat your current baseline, backtested honestly before anyone plans against them.
overview: Every company forecasts, mostly in spreadsheets: last year plus a percentage. The question is not whether ML can forecast, it is whether it beats what you do today by enough to change decisions: stock levels, staffing, cash planning, risk limits. We start every forecasting engagement by measuring your current baseline, because that is the number to beat.

The work runs on backtesting: models are trained on your history and evaluated as if they had been running for the past year, quarter by quarter, with only the information you had at the time. No leakage, no cherry-picked windows. You see error metrics per product, region or segment before anything touches planning.

In production, forecasts arrive on schedule through an API or straight into your planning tables, with uncertainty ranges rather than single numbers. Monitoring compares forecasts against actuals as they land and flags degradation early, and retraining is a scheduled pipeline rather than a rescue project.

Engagements usually start with an audit: how models reach production today, where the manual steps hide and what breaks first under load or drift. From there we install the missing pieces in priority order: versioned data and models, CI that runs evals on every change, deployment with rollback, and monitoring tied to alerts someone actually receives.

The goal is that shipping a model change becomes as routine as shipping code. Your team ends up with a paved road: a retrain is a pipeline run, a rollback is one command, and an audit question is answered from the model registry instead of from somebody's memory. We stay until your engineers run that road without us.

Your batch warehouse and the streaming path share definitions, so the live number and tomorrow's report finally agree. faq.q: Do we need an AI strategy before running a pilot?
faq.a: Not always. If one use case is obviously valuable, a pilot first is fine and we often recommend it. Strategy earns its cost when there are many candidate ideas, several stakeholders and a real budget decision to make.

faq.q: Who from our side needs to be involved?
faq.a: A sponsor from leadership, the owners of the affected workflows, and someone who knows your systems and data. Expect a handful of interviews and two workshops: a few hours per person over the whole engagement, not weeks of their time.

faq.q: What if the honest answer is that AI is not worth it yet?
faq.a: Then that is the recommendation you get, in writing, with the reasons. Usually there is a prerequisite worth fixing first, like data access or process consistency, and the roadmap says exactly when AI becomes worth revisiting.

ai-readiness-audit.subtitle: A two-week, fixed-fee audit of your data, systems, team and processes. Ends in a scorecard and a plan for the gaps that actually matter.
overview: The readiness audit answers one question: what stands between your organization and a working AI system in production? We review your data quality and access, your integration surface, your security and compliance constraints, and your team's skills, all measured against the use cases you actually want to ship, not a generic checklist.

It runs in two weeks at a fixed fee. We hold structured interviews with your engineering, data and business leads, inspect the systems involved hands-on where access allows, and test a sample of your data against the requirements of your target use cases. You get findings backed by direct inspection, not questionnaire answers.

You walk away with a readiness scorecard across data, systems, people and governance, plus a gap plan that separates blockers from nice-to-haves. Most clients find they are closer than they thought: the gaps are usually specific and fixable rather than structural, and they rarely stop a first pilot from starting within the quarter.

ai-governance.title: Data & AI governance
ai-governance.subtitle: Who owns which data, who may see it, how long you keep it, and what the GDPR and the EU AI Act require of every AI use. Set up so it does not stall your roadmap.
overview: Governance starts with the data, not the model. We map where each dataset comes from, who owns it, who may see it, how long you are allowed to keep it and where it flows next. Most companies discover here that the same customer record lives in four systems under three different retention rules, and that is the finding that makes the rest of the work possible.

On top of that we classify your AI use cases under the EU AI Act, set up the risk assessments and documentation each class requires, and write the policies that matter for your exposure: personal-data handling and the GDPR basis for it, human oversight, model documentation, incident response. The engagement starts with an inventory of every AI system, use case and vendor tool in play, including the unofficial ones your teams already use. The checks are wired into your existing delivery process, not into a parallel bureaucracy.

What changes: your compliance and legal teams get evidence they can hand to auditors or to a data protection authority, and your engineers get clear rules instead of case-by-case escalation. New AI initiatives clear governance in days rather than weeks, because the gates, the data map and the templates already exist and everyone involved knows how to use them.

faq.q: Does the EU AI Act even apply to us?
faq.a: If you operate in the EU and use AI in products, hiring, credit, safety or anything customer-facing, parts of it almost certainly do. The inventory and classification give you a definitive answer per use case instead of a general worry.

faq.q: Will governance slow our delivery down?
faq.a: Done badly, yes. That is why we wire the gates into your existing workflow and size them by risk. Low-risk uses get a lightweight checklist, and heavy review is reserved for the few systems that genuinely warrant it.

faq.q: We already have a compliance team. Why involve engineers?
faq.a: Because the obligations land in code: logging, oversight hooks, documentation, evaluation evidence. We translate legal requirements into technical controls your compliance team can verify, which is the part most policy documents skip.

faq.q: Is this about the AI Act or about the GDPR?
faq.a: Both, and separating them wastes your time. An AI use case almost always processes personal data, so it needs a lawful basis, a retention rule and an access model under the GDPR, and a risk classification with its documentation under the AI Act. We work through them together, per use case, and you end up with one set of evidence instead of two projects that contradict each other.

We train your engineers, product managers and leadership on the AI skills their roles actually need, working on your codebase and your data rather than toy examples. The goal is a team that scopes, builds and operates AI features without external help, and knows when to ask for it.

Formats match the audience: hands-on workshops for engineers covering retrieval (RAG), accuracy testing, prompting and automation patterns; use-case and scoping sessions for product teams; briefings for leadership on cost, risk and realistic timelines. Sessions run on your stack, and every exercise leaves working code or a usable artifact behind, not just notes.

What changes: AI stops being one specialist's domain. Engineers ship LLM features with evals attached, product managers write AI specs that survive contact with reality, and leadership makes fund-or-kill decisions on real numbers. Internal champions carry the practice forward after we leave, which is the point of the whole exercise.

react.title: React
react.subtitle: Complex, long-lived web interfaces built by senior engineers: AI-accelerated delivery, strict TypeScript, and performance treated as a requirement.
overview: React is our default for interfaces where the complexity lives in the UI itself: SaaS products, data-heavy dashboards, internal tools with hundreds of screens, and design systems shared across products. We build these as strict TypeScript codebases with component libraries your team can extend without us.

We are honest about fit. React earns its cost when the interface is stateful, interactive and expected to live for years; the ecosystem and hiring pool are unmatched, and the codebase survives team changes. For content-first sites where SEO and first load dominate, we usually recommend Next.js instead, and for a simple brochure site React is overkill. We will say so before you spend money on it.

Delivery is AI-accelerated: our engineers use tools like Claude Code to move faster on scaffolding, tests and refactors, and a senior engineer reviews every change before it merges. The speed comes from the tooling; the quality comes from the review gate, the test suite and the performance budgets enforced in CI.

benefits.title: An ecosystem that outlives trends
benefits.description: React has the largest hiring pool and library ecosystem in frontend. A React codebase written to standards stays maintainable after we hand it over, and after your team changes.

benefits.title: Honest fit, checked by builders
benefits.description: The engineers scoping your project are the ones who would build it. If React is the wrong tool for your case, you hear that in the first call, not after the invoice.

benefits.title: AI speed, senior judgment
benefits.description: AI tooling accelerates the mechanical work; senior engineers own the architecture, review every merge and write the tests that keep speed from turning into debt.

benefits.title: Performance as a requirement
benefits.description: Bundle-size budgets, code splitting and render profiling are part of the definition of done, not a rescue project after launch.

approach.title: Scope and architecture
approach.description: We map the screens, states and data flows, then fix the decisions that are expensive to change later: state management, routing, API contracts and the component model.

approach.title: Build in vertical slices
approach.description: Each sprint ships a working end-to-end feature, not a layer. You see the real product in a preview environment from week one and correct course while it is cheap.

approach.title: Review, test, measure
approach.description: Every pull request passes senior review, automated tests (unit, component, Playwright end-to-end) and the performance budget before it merges. No exceptions under deadline pressure.

approach.title: Harden and hand over
approach.description: Before launch we profile renders, audit accessibility, close the documentation and walk your team through the codebase until they can extend it without us.

deliverables: Production React application in strict TypeScript
Component library documented in Storybook
Automated test suite: unit, component and end-to-end
CI/CD pipeline with preview deployments per pull request
Performance and accessibility audit with fixes applied
Architecture decision records and handover documentation

faq.q: Is React the right choice for our project?
faq.a: It depends on where the complexity sits. Stateful, interactive product UIs: yes. Content-first sites where SEO and load time dominate: usually Next.js. A five-page marketing site: neither, a lighter stack costs less to run. You get that assessment in the first call, free.

faq.q: Does AI-generated code hurt quality?
faq.a: Not in our process. AI tooling drafts the repetitive parts; a senior engineer reviews every line before merge, and nothing ships without passing tests and the performance budget. You get the speed without inheriting unreviewed code.

faq.q: Can you take over an existing React codebase?
faq.a: Yes, and it is common work for us. We start with a short audit: dependency health, test coverage, render performance and the state management story. You get a prioritized fix list, then we either execute it or hand it to your team.

faq.q: React or Next.js?
faq.a: React is the library; Next.js is a framework built on it. If you need server rendering, SEO, or a content site and a product in one codebase, go Next.js. If you are building a pure app behind a login, plain React with Vite is often simpler. We use both and pick per project.

nextjs.label: Technologies
nextjs.title: Next.js
nextjs.subtitle: Marketing site and product in one codebase: server-rendered, fast by default and measured against Core Web Vitals in CI.
overview: Next.js is what we reach for when a project needs to be found, load fast and still behave like a product: marketing sites on a headless CMS, SaaS applications, e-commerce storefronts and full-stack apps built on server components and API routes. Our own website runs on Next.js with a headless CMS, so we ship on the stack we sell.

It is the right choice when SEO and first load matter, when content and application share one codebase, or when you want rendering decided per page: static where possible, server-rendered where needed, client-side where it earns it. It is the wrong choice for a pure internal tool behind a login, where plain React with Vite is simpler to build and cheaper to run; we will tell you which side of that line you are on.

Delivery is AI-accelerated with a senior review gate: engineers use AI tooling for scaffolding, migrations and test coverage, and every change passes review, automated tests and a Core Web Vitals budget in CI before it merges. We deploy to Vercel or to your own infrastructure in containers; the codebase does not lock you to a host.

benefits.title: SEO and speed without a second stack
benefits.description: Server rendering and static generation come from the same codebase as your product. No separate marketing site drifting out of sync.

benefits.title: Rendering decided per page
benefits.description: Static, server or client rendering is chosen where each pays off, so you are not paying server costs for pages that never change, or shipping JavaScript nobody needs.

benefits.title: No host lock-in
benefits.description: We build Next.js to run on Vercel or in containers on your cloud. The deployment decision stays reversible.

benefits.title: Web Vitals enforced in CI
benefits.description: Performance budgets fail the build, not the postmortem. Regressions get caught in a pull request, not in your search rankings.

approach.title: Architecture and rendering map
approach.description: We inventory pages and features, then decide the rendering mode per route, the caching strategy and the CMS content model before writing feature code.

approach.title: Build with previews
approach.description: Every pull request gets a preview deployment your team can click through. Content editors work in the CMS in parallel from an early stage.

approach.title: Quality gates
approach.description: Senior review, Playwright end-to-end tests and Lighthouse budgets run in CI on every change. AI accelerates the writing; the gates stay non-negotiable.

approach.title: Launch and measure
approach.description: We launch with redirects, sitemaps, structured data and analytics wired in, then verify Core Web Vitals on live traffic and fix what the field data disproves.

Headless CMS integration with an editorial workflow
Technical SEO setup: metadata, sitemaps, redirects and structured data
CI/CD pipeline with preview deployments and Core Web Vitals budgets

faq.q: Do we need Vercel to run Next.js?
faq.a: No. Vercel is the smoothest path and often the right one, but we regularly deploy Next.js in Docker containers on AWS and other clouds. We model the hosting cost both ways and let the numbers decide.

faq.q: Can you migrate our existing site to Next.js?
faq.a: Yes, incrementally: URL inventory and redirect map first, then sections move one at a time behind a proxy so rankings and traffic carry over. A big-bang rewrite is almost never necessary.

faq.q: Next.js or plain React?
faq.a: If SEO, content or server rendering matter: Next.js. An internal application behind a login: usually React with Vite. We use both; the choice is made per project and justified in writing.

faq.q: Which CMS do you pair it with?
faq.a: Usually Payload, which runs our own site, or a headless CMS your team already knows. The criteria are editorial workflow, self-hosting requirements and licensing cost; we recommend after seeing your content model.

vue.label: Technologies
vue.title: Vue
vue.subtitle: Pragmatic frontends in Vue 3 and Nuxt: approachable for your team, strict about types, tests and performance.
overview: With Vue we build single-page applications, admin dashboards, Nuxt websites and interactive components embedded in existing server-rendered apps on Laravel, Rails or .NET. We also run Vue 2 to Vue 3 migrations for teams whose codebases outlived the framework version they were built on.

Vue is the right choice when your team already runs on it, when you want one cohesive framework with official routing, state and tooling instead of assembling an ecosystem yourself, or when you are adding rich interactivity to a server-rendered application without rewriting it. It is the weaker choice if you need code shared with React Native or if your local hiring market is overwhelmingly React; we will tell you honestly which applies.

We work in Vue 3 with the Composition API and strict TypeScript: Pinia for state, Vitest and Playwright for tests, Nuxt where server rendering or SEO matter. Delivery is AI-accelerated, with a senior engineer reviewing every merge; Vue work at pluscode passes the same review, testing and performance gates as our React work.

benefits.title: One cohesive stack, officially maintained
benefits.description: Router, Pinia and Vite are first-party. Fewer integration decisions, fewer abandoned dependencies, faster onboarding for new engineers.

benefits.title: Plays well with what you have
benefits.description: Vue mounts cleanly inside existing server-rendered pages, so you can modernize a Laravel or Rails app screen by screen instead of betting on a rewrite.

benefits.title: A clean exit from Vue 2
benefits.description: Vue 2 is end-of-life. We migrate to Vue 3 incrementally, with a compatibility build and a test harness, so the product keeps shipping during the migration.

benefits.title: The same engineering bar
benefits.description: Strict TypeScript, senior review on every merge, automated tests and performance budgets. Framework choice never lowers the standard.

approach.title: Assess
approach.description: Greenfield or existing codebase, we start by mapping the state model, the component boundaries and, for migrations, everything pinned to Vue 2 APIs.

approach.title: Architect
approach.description: We fix the decisions that hurt to change later: Pinia store design, routing, TypeScript strictness, and whether Nuxt earns its place in your case.

approach.title: Build and review
approach.description: AI tooling accelerates components, tests and refactors; a senior engineer reviews every pull request before merge. Working software lands in a preview environment every sprint.

approach.title: Stabilize and hand over
approach.description: We close test coverage, profile performance, document the architecture and walk your team through the codebase until they own it comfortably.

Typed Pinia stores and a documented component library
Vue 2 to Vue 3 migration plan and executed migration, where relevant
Automated test suite: Vitest unit tests and Playwright end-to-end
CI/CD pipeline with preview deployments
Architecture documentation and handover sessions

faq.q: Is Vue a safe long-term bet?
faq.a: Yes. Vue 3 is actively developed, backed by a stable core team and used at scale across Europe and Asia. The real risk is staying on Vue 2, which is end-of-life; if that is you, migration is the first thing to plan.

faq.q: We are on Vue 2. Rewrite or migrate?
faq.a: Migrate, almost always. The migration build lets you move incrementally, and a test harness catches regressions as you go. We scope it with a short audit: most codebases take weeks, not months, and the product keeps shipping meanwhile.

faq.q: Vue or React?
faq.a: If your team knows Vue or you are extending a server-rendered app: Vue. If you need the largest hiring pool or React Native code sharing: React. Both clear our quality bar; the decision is about your team and constraints, and you get our recommendation in writing.

faq.q: When do you add Nuxt?
faq.a: When server rendering, SEO or file-based routing across a content-heavy site pay their way. For a pure SPA behind a login, plain Vue with Vite stays simpler.

angular.label: Technologies
angular.title: Angular
angular.subtitle: Enterprise frontends built to stay maintainable for a decade: strict typing, enforced conventions and upgrades that never turn into rewrites.
overview: With Angular we build the applications companies run their operations on: large internal platforms, forms-heavy business systems, regulated-industry frontends and multi-team codebases organized in Nx monorepos. We also modernize aging Angular estates, from AngularJS remnants to apps stuck several major versions behind.

Angular is the right choice when multiple teams share one codebase over many years and you want the framework, not folklore, to enforce structure: dependency injection, a batteries-included router and forms, and an upgrade path managed by Google. It is the wrong choice for marketing sites, content-first SEO plays or quick MVPs, where Next.js or a lighter stack ships faster; if that describes your project, we will point you there instead.

We build modern Angular: standalone components, signals, strict TypeScript and OnPush change detection as defaults, not aspirations. Delivery is AI-accelerated with a senior review gate on every merge, tests in Vitest or Jest plus Playwright, and budgets on bundle size and change detection cost enforced in CI.

benefits.title: Structure that scales across teams
benefits.description: Angular's conventions and dependency injection keep ten teams in one monorepo writing code that looks the same. Less bikeshedding, cheaper onboarding, easier audits.

benefits.title: Modern Angular, not 2016 Angular
benefits.description: Signals, standalone components and typed forms have changed the framework. We build with current Angular and clear the legacy patterns out of existing code.

benefits.title: Upgrades as routine, not events
benefits.description: We keep apps within one major version of current using Angular's update tooling and schematics. Boring, scheduled upgrades beat a forced rewrite in year five.

benefits.title: Complex forms under control
benefits.description: Typed reactive forms, validation logic and RxJS data flows built to be unit-tested, so workflows with 200 fields stay changeable years later.

approach.title: Audit or blueprint
approach.description: For existing estates we audit versions, patterns and test coverage; for new builds we lay out the Nx workspace, module boundaries and data flow before feature work starts.

approach.title: Modernize incrementally
approach.description: Upgrades and refactors ship in small, releasable steps alongside feature delivery. The application keeps working every day of the engagement.

approach.title: Build with gates
approach.description: AI tooling accelerates components, migrations and specs; every merge passes senior review, tests and budgets in CI. Framework discipline is enforced by machines, not memos.

approach.title: Hand over an operating model
approach.description: You get documentation, architecture decision records and an upgrade calendar, plus pairing sessions so your team maintains the standard after we leave.

deliverables: Production Angular application on a current major version
Nx workspace with enforced module boundaries, where team size warrants it
Modernization roadmap and executed upgrades for existing estates
Automated test suite: unit, component and Playwright end-to-end
CI/CD pipeline with performance and bundle-size budgets
Architecture decision records and an upgrade playbook

faq.q: Is Angular still a good choice?
faq.a: For its niche, yes. Google develops it actively, releases on a predictable schedule, and signals plus standalone components have modernized it substantially. For large, long-lived, multi-team applications it remains one of the strongest options; for content sites and MVPs we recommend other stacks.

faq.q: We are several versions behind. Rewrite or upgrade?
faq.a: Upgrade, in almost every case. Angular's tooling automates much of each major-version step, and we do them incrementally while your roadmap continues. A rewrite is only on the table for AngularJS (1.x) codebases, and even there we usually migrate screen by screen, not big-bang.

faq.q: Angular or React?
faq.a: Angular buys enforced consistency for large or rotating teams on decade-scale systems; React buys flexibility and a larger hiring pool. We build with both, and our recommendation follows your team structure and time horizon, in writing.

faq.q: Does AI-accelerated development work with Angular?
faq.a: Especially well. Angular's strong conventions make AI output predictable, and strict typing means deviations fail the build. Repetitive work accelerates most: specs, form scaffolding, version migrations. The gate stays senior review on every merge.

python.label: Technologies
python.title: Python
python.subtitle: AI services, data pipelines and production APIs. The language our AI work ships in, written by senior engineers and reviewed like code that has to run for years.
overview: Python is where most of our AI and data engineering ships. We build LLM applications and RAG systems, model serving and evaluation infrastructure, the data pipelines that feed them, and the FastAPI or Django services that expose it all to the rest of your stack. If the project touches machine learning, its core is almost certainly Python.

It is the right choice when the work involves AI, data processing or fast-moving product APIs: the ecosystem (PyTorch, LangGraph, pandas, Airflow) is unmatched and senior Python engineers are easy to hire. It is the wrong choice for CPU-bound hot paths with strict latency budgets or for teams standardized on the JVM; in those cases we say so and recommend Java, Node.js or a mixed architecture instead.

We develop AI-accelerated: engineers use AI tooling to move fast, and every line still passes senior review before it merges. Type hints and mypy across the codebase, tests wired into CI from day one, and tracing, metrics and structured logs in place before go-live. Speed comes from the tooling; reliability comes from the discipline.

benefits.title: The default language of AI
benefits.description: Every model, framework and vector database ships Python bindings first. Building AI in Python means using the tools the way their authors intended, not through a second-class wrapper.

benefits.title: From idea to API in days
benefits.description: FastAPI plus the Python ecosystem turns a well-scoped feature into a documented, tested endpoint fast. Product teams iterate weekly, not quarterly.

benefits.title: One language across the data path
benefits.description: Ingestion, transformation, training, serving and the API in front of it can share one language, one test suite and one deployment story. Fewer handoffs, fewer bugs at the seams.

benefits.title: An honest performance profile
benefits.description: Python is fast enough for the vast majority of API workloads, and we prove it with load tests. Where it is not, we isolate the hot path and move it, instead of pretending the problem is not there.

approach.title: Scope and architecture
approach.description: Before any code, we agree what the service must do, at what latency and volume. Architecture decisions (framework, data stores, async or not) are written down with the reasons.

approach.title: AI-accelerated build
approach.description: Engineers use AI tooling for the mechanical parts and their judgment where it matters. Every pull request is reviewed by a senior engineer before merge, no exceptions.

approach.title: Tests and types as guardrails
approach.description: Type checking and tests run in CI on every commit. Data pipelines get contract tests, model-facing code gets evaluation runs; regressions are caught before deploy, not after.

approach.title: Observability and handover
approach.description: Structured logs, metrics and tracing ship with the service, not after it. We hand over runbooks and walk your team through the codebase, so you are not dependent on us.

deliverables: Production services in FastAPI or Django, typed and senior-reviewed
Data pipelines with orchestration, monitoring and alerting
A test suite and CI/CD pipeline that gate every change
OpenAPI documentation your teams can build against
Dashboards, tracing and structured logging from day one

faq.q: Is Python fast enough for production APIs?
faq.a: For most workloads, yes, and we verify it with load tests against your actual traffic profile rather than benchmarks from the internet. Async FastAPI handles thousands of requests per second on modest hardware. When a specific path is genuinely CPU-bound, we isolate it and move that piece, not the whole system.

faq.q: FastAPI or Django?
faq.a: FastAPI for API-first services and anything touching ML; Django when you need the batteries: admin, auth, ORM and years of proven patterns for content-heavy products. We pick per project and tell you why in writing. Both are boring, well-supported choices, which is exactly what you want.

faq.q: Can you take over an existing Python codebase?
faq.a: Yes. We start with a short audit: dependency health, test coverage, typing, deployment. You get a prioritized list of risks before we commit to a roadmap. Most codebases need less rewriting than their owners fear; we fix what blocks delivery and leave the rest.

faq.q: Does AI-generated code lower the quality bar?
faq.a: No, because the bar is enforced by process, not by who typed the code. Everything passes senior review, type checks and tests before merge. AI tooling changes how fast a candidate change appears; it changes nothing about what we accept.

ruby-on-rails.subtitle: The fastest route from product idea to paying customers. One framework, one small senior team, working software in weeks.
ruby-on-rails.overviewTitle: What we build with Ruby on Rails
overview: Rails is our tool for rapid product development: SaaS products, marketplaces, internal platforms and customer portals that need to exist in weeks, not quarters. One framework covers the database, the business logic, the background jobs and, with Hotwire, most of the frontend, so a small senior team ships the whole product.

It is the right choice when speed to market decides the outcome: an MVP that has to meet real users this quarter, a product still searching for its shape, a CRUD-heavy B2B tool. It is the wrong choice for compute-heavy workloads, ML cores or teams that need a typed language at large scale; there we reach for Python, Node.js or Java and say so early.

We develop AI-accelerated: AI tooling handles the boilerplate Rails already minimizes, and senior engineers review every change before merge. A full RSpec test suite, CI/CD from the first week, and monitoring and error tracking live before your first user notices anything. Rails gave the speed its reputation; the discipline is what keeps it.

benefits.title: Weeks to first users
benefits.description: Convention over configuration means no time lost on decisions that do not matter. Auth, payments, admin and background jobs are solved problems; the attention goes into your product logic.

benefits.title: A codebase one team can hold
benefits.description: Rails keeps the whole product in one repository, one language, one mental model. A small senior team stays productive where a microservice stack needs a platoon.

benefits.title: Proven at real scale
benefits.description: Shopify, GitHub and Basecamp run on Rails. The scaling ceiling sits far above the point where most products succeed or fail, and the path toward it is well documented.

benefits.title: Cheap to change
benefits.description: Early products pivot. Rails makes schema changes, new flows and rebuilt screens routine work, so the cost of learning from your users stays low.

approach.title: Scope the first release
approach.description: We cut the idea down to the smallest product that can meet real users, and define what it must prove. The first two weeks end in running software, not documents.

approach.title: Build with AI, review by seniors
approach.description: AI tooling accelerates the routine work; every pull request still passes a senior engineer's review before merge. The velocity is real and so is the code quality.

approach.title: Test what matters
approach.description: System and model tests in RSpec cover the flows your revenue depends on. CI runs everything on every push; broken builds do not reach production.

approach.title: Launch and iterate
approach.description: Deployment, monitoring and error tracking are set up before launch. After launch we ship in weekly cycles, driven by what real usage shows.

A Hotwire frontend, with no separate SPA to maintain
An RSpec test suite covering the critical flows
A CI/CD pipeline with one-command deploys

faq.q: Is Rails still a safe bet in 2026?
faq.a: Yes. Rails 8 ships actively, the framework runs some of the largest revenue-producing codebases on the web, and hiring senior Rails engineers is easier than the noise suggests. Frameworks die from abandonment, not from age; Rails has neither problem.

faq.q: Will it scale if the product takes off?
faq.a: Rails scales further than most products ever need: Shopify handles peak sales events on it. The scaling work is real but well-trodden: caching, job queues, read replicas, extracting hot services once the numbers justify it. We architect so the first bottleneck is far away and measurable.

faq.q: Can we add AI features to a Rails product?
faq.a: Yes, and we do it constantly. The product lives in Rails; AI-heavy pieces run as Python services behind an internal API, or call model providers directly where that is enough. You get Rails speed for the product and the right tool for the AI, with no compromise on either side.

faq.q: What does an MVP actually cost?
faq.a: Most well-scoped MVPs land in the six to twelve week range with a two or three person senior team. After a scoping call you get a fixed quote with milestones, not an hourly estimate with no ceiling. If the scope is too big for that, we tell you what to cut and why.

nodejs.label: Technologies
nodejs.title: Node.js
nodejs.subtitle: Real-time APIs and full-stack TypeScript. One language from the browser to the backend, built for thousands of concurrent connections.
overview: We use Node.js for real-time systems and full-stack TypeScript products: WebSocket backends for chat, collaboration and live dashboards, event-driven APIs, backend-for-frontend layers, and products where Next.js on the frontend and NestJS or Fastify on the backend share one language and one type system.

It is the right choice when the workload is I/O-heavy and concurrent (many connections, many API calls, little computation per request), when your team already lives in TypeScript, or when serverless economics matter. It is the wrong choice for CPU-heavy processing and ML workloads; there we pair it with Python or Java services and keep Node doing what it is best at.

We develop AI-accelerated, with senior review on every merge. Strict TypeScript across the codebase, contract tests between frontend and backend, load tests on the real-time paths, and tracing, metrics and structured logs before launch. The event loop is fast; our process makes sure your system is also correct.

benefits.title: One language, one team
benefits.description: Shared types between client and server remove a whole class of integration bugs and let one team own a feature end to end. No handoff between frontend and backend guilds.

benefits.title: Built for concurrent I/O
benefits.description: The event loop holds tens of thousands of open connections on a single node. For chat, live updates and API aggregation, that is the exact shape of the problem.

benefits.title: The largest ecosystem there is
benefits.description: npm has a maintained library for nearly everything, and hiring TypeScript engineers is as easy as hiring gets. Your future team options stay open.

benefits.title: Serverless and edge native
benefits.description: Fast cold starts make Node the default runtime of every major serverless and edge platform. You pay for usage instead of idle servers, where the workload fits.

approach.title: Design the contracts first
approach.description: We define API and event contracts up front, as TypeScript types shared between services. The architecture (REST, WebSockets, queues) is chosen against your latency and volume numbers, not out of habit.

approach.title: AI-accelerated build, senior review
approach.description: AI tooling generates the routine parts fast; senior engineers review every pull request and own the hard decisions. Strict compiler settings are non-negotiable.

approach.title: Test where it can break
approach.description: Unit and integration tests in CI, contract tests on service boundaries, load tests on the real-time paths that carry your traffic. Every merge is gated.

approach.title: Ship with observability
approach.description: Tracing, metrics, structured logs and alerting are wired in before go-live, plus runbooks and a handover for your team. You see what production is doing from day one.

deliverables: Production TypeScript services in NestJS or Fastify
A real-time layer (WebSockets or server-sent events) load-tested at your target concurrency
Shared type packages consumed by frontend and backend
A CI/CD pipeline with tests gating every merge
OpenAPI or event schema documentation
Dashboards, tracing and alerting configured for production

faq.q: JavaScript or TypeScript?
faq.a: TypeScript, strictly configured, without exception. On anything larger than a prototype the type system pays for itself within weeks: faster reviews and regressions that never happen. We treat plain JavaScript backends as legacy and migrate them incrementally.

faq.q: Is Node.js fast enough for our backend?
faq.a: For I/O-bound workloads Node is excellent: thousands of concurrent requests per node at low latency. It is the wrong tool for heavy per-request computation; if profiling shows a CPU-bound core, we move that piece to a worker, a queue or another runtime, and we say so before you commit.

faq.q: Which framework do you use?
faq.a: NestJS when a large codebase needs structure a team can follow; Fastify when raw throughput and a small footprint matter; Next.js API routes only for small backends that live inside the app itself. We recommend per project, in writing, with the reasons.

faq.q: Can you work inside our existing stack?
faq.a: Yes. Most Node work we do lands inside an existing product: a real-time layer beside a REST API, a BFF in front of legacy services, an extracted service where the monolith hurts. We start with an audit of the current state and integrate rather than rewrite where possible.

cta.subtitle: Book a free 30-minute call with a senior engineer. You leave knowing whether Node.js fits your workload and what the first milestone should be.

java.label: Technologies
java.title: Java
java.subtitle: Enterprise backends that run for a decade. Spring Boot services, high-volume transaction systems and the integrations regulated businesses depend on.
overview: We build Java where reliability is the requirement, not a preference: transactional backends for finance, logistics and insurance, Spring Boot services in large system landscapes, Kafka-based event processing, and integrations with the systems enterprises actually run, from SAP to twenty-year-old SOAP services.

It is the right choice for long-lived systems, strict compliance environments, sustained high throughput and organizations already invested in the JVM. It is the wrong choice for a two-person startup racing to a first release; there Rails or Node.js gets you to market faster, and we will tell you that in the first call.

We develop AI-accelerated, with senior review on every merge, which removes most of the ceremony Java is blamed for. Modern Java (21 and newer, records, virtual threads), automated tests at every level, and observability with OpenTelemetry as part of the definition of done. The result reads like Java written by people who like the language.

benefits.title: Built for systems that cannot fail
benefits.description: Static typing, a mature toolchain and thirty years of production hardening catch whole classes of errors before deploy. For money movements and contracts, that margin matters.

benefits.title: Performance under sustained load
benefits.description: The JVM's JIT and virtual threads carry high-throughput, long-running workloads with predictable latency. Not the fastest language to prototype in; very hard to beat at month twelve under load.

benefits.title: At home in the enterprise
benefits.description: Security standards, audit trails, SSO, message queues and legacy protocols are solved problems in the Java ecosystem. Your compliance team will not be meeting them for the first time.

benefits.title: A talent pool that lasts
benefits.description: Java engineers exist in every market at every seniority level. A system we hand over will find maintainers for the next fifteen years, which is not true of every stack.

approach.title: Understand the landscape
approach.description: Enterprise systems fail at the boundaries, so we start there: the systems to integrate, the contracts, the compliance constraints, the load profile. Architecture is documented and defended before code.

approach.title: AI-accelerated build, senior review
approach.description: AI tooling eliminates Java's boilerplate cost; senior engineers review every merge and own every design decision. Velocity without the usual enterprise drag.

approach.title: Test at every level
approach.description: Unit, integration and contract tests, plus load tests against the agreed throughput targets, all gating CI. For event-driven systems we test the failure modes, not just the happy paths.

approach.title: Operate and hand over
approach.description: Metrics, tracing and alerting via OpenTelemetry, runbooks for your operations team, and a structured handover. We stay for the first production weeks, then leave you independent.

Event processing on Kafka where the architecture calls for it
Integration adapters for your existing system landscape
A test pyramid wired into CI/CD, including load tests
OpenTelemetry-based observability with dashboards and alerts
Architecture decision records and runbooks your teams can operate from

faq.q: Isn't Java slow to develop in?
faq.a: That reputation comes from Java 6 and heavyweight process, not from the language today. Records, virtual threads and Spring Boot removed most of the ceremony, and AI-accelerated development removes most of what was left. Our Java delivery pace surprises teams who last saw the language a decade ago.

faq.q: Spring Boot or something newer?
faq.a: Spring Boot by default: it is the ecosystem your future hires know and your systems integrate with. Quarkus or plain Java where cold starts or footprint genuinely matter, such as serverless. We choose per workload and put the reasoning in the architecture record.

faq.q: Can you modernize our legacy Java system?
faq.a: Yes, incrementally. We audit first, then modernize in slices: upgrade the runtime, put tests around the critical paths, extract services only where the evidence supports it. Big-bang rewrites of working enterprise systems fail often enough that we do not recommend them.

faq.q: Java or Kotlin?
faq.a: Both run on the JVM and interoperate cleanly, so this is a team question more than a technical one. Modern Java has closed much of the gap. We default to Java for the wider hiring pool; if your codebase or team already lives in Kotlin, we work in Kotlin.

ios-swift.label: Technologies
ios-swift.title: iOS (Swift)
ios-swift.subtitle: Native iOS development in Swift and SwiftUI: apps that feel like Apple built them, run fast on every iPhone, and clear App Store review without drama.
overview: We design and build native iOS apps in Swift, with SwiftUI as the default UI framework and UIKit where a specific screen demands it. Native means direct access to everything the platform offers: new APIs on launch day, the full performance of Apple silicon, and interface patterns your users already know from every other app on their phone.

The economics matter as much as the engineering. Native is the right call when the app is core to your business, when performance and polish drive retention, or when you need deep platform features: camera pipelines, Bluetooth, HealthKit, widgets, Live Activities, App Intents, or machine learning on the device itself. If a cross-platform build would serve you better, we say so in the first call; we build with React Native and Flutter too, so the recommendation is not self-serving.

Delivery includes the part most teams underestimate: getting through App Store review. We build against Apple's guidelines from the first sprint, ship weekly TestFlight builds to your stakeholders, prepare the listing and privacy labels, and manage submission, reviewer questions and the phased rollout. Most of our submissions pass on the first attempt, because rejection reasons get engineered out early instead of patched at the end.

benefits.title: UX that matches the platform
benefits.description: SwiftUI plus Apple's Human Interface Guidelines produce apps that behave the way iPhone users expect: navigation, gestures, haptics, Dynamic Type and dark mode are correct by construction, not approximated by a rendering layer.

benefits.title: Performance users can feel
benefits.description: Compiled Swift, no JavaScript bridge, full use of Apple silicon. We profile with Instruments, set budgets for cold start, 120 Hz scroll smoothness and memory, and hold every release to them.

benefits.title: On-device AI without the round trip
benefits.description: Core ML and the Neural Engine run models directly on the phone: text extraction, image classification, speech, custom models. Features work offline, respond in milliseconds and keep user data on the device, which simplifies both GDPR and your privacy label.

benefits.title: New OS features on day one
benefits.description: Widgets, Live Activities, App Intents and each year's WWDC additions are available to native apps immediately. Your app can use them the day the OS ships, not after a plugin catches up.

approach.title: Design for the platform
approach.description: Screens are designed against the Human Interface Guidelines from the first wireframe, not converted from a web layout. Every flow is prototyped and reviewed on real devices.

approach.title: Build in weekly increments
approach.description: Weekly TestFlight builds from the first sprint: you see progress on your own phone, and feedback lands in the next build. CI runs the full XCTest suite and static analysis on every merge.

approach.title: Ship and stabilize
approach.description: We prepare the App Store listing, privacy labels and review notes, manage submission and any reviewer questions, then roll out in phases while watching crash rates and performance metrics before going to 100 percent.

faq.a: When the app is central to your business, when performance and platform feel drive retention, or when you need deep hardware and OS integration: camera, Bluetooth, HealthKit, widgets, on-device ML. For a content app or an MVP testing demand on both platforms, cross-platform is often the better spend, and we will tell you which case you are in during the first call.

faq.q: How do you handle App Store review and rejections?
faq.a: We build against the review guidelines from sprint one: no gray-area API use, correct purchase flows, privacy labels that match the code. We write the review notes, submit, and answer the reviewer directly. If a rejection happens, the fix is on us; most of our submissions pass first time.

faq.q: Can you take over an existing iOS app?
faq.a: Yes. We start with a code audit: architecture, test coverage, crash rate, dependency health. You get a written assessment and a plan. A typical takeover modernizes incrementally, Objective-C to Swift and UIKit to SwiftUI screen by screen, while features keep shipping, instead of a rewrite that freezes your roadmap.

faq.q: What can on-device AI actually do today?
faq.a: Quite a lot: text recognition, image and document classification, speech transcription, semantic search, and custom Core ML models. It runs offline, costs nothing per request and keeps data on the phone. For generative features we combine on-device models with server-side LLMs, routing by task, cost and privacy.

react-native.label: Technologies
react-native.title: React Native
react-native.subtitle: One TypeScript codebase for iOS and Android, built by engineers who know exactly where the framework ends and native code begins.
overview: React Native lets one team ship iOS and Android from a single TypeScript codebase, with 85 to 95 percent of the code shared in a typical business app. That is the economics in one sentence: one backlog, one release train, and every feature lands in both stores at the same time instead of being built twice and slowly drifting apart.

It wins most often when you already have React on the web. Your engineers know the component model, the state patterns and the tooling on day one, and the design system and business logic you built for the browser carry over to mobile. No other cross-platform stack converts an existing web team into a mobile team this cheaply, and the React hiring pool is the largest in the industry when you grow.

It is not native code, and we do not pretend it is. Camera pipelines, Bluetooth, widgets and heavy real-time graphics still mean writing Swift and Kotlin modules, and every React Native upgrade costs real engineering time. We scope that boundary before the project starts, budget the maintenance honestly, and tell you plainly when your app would be better served by Flutter or two native codebases.

benefits.title: One codebase, two stores
benefits.description: A typical business app shares 85 to 95 percent of its code. You fund one team and one backlog, and iOS and Android ship the same features on the same day.

benefits.title: Your web team is your mobile team
benefits.description: React Native is React with native building blocks. Engineers who ship your web app are productive in the mobile codebase within days, not months.

benefits.title: Fixes without the store queue
benefits.description: Over-the-air updates push JavaScript-level fixes directly to users, within store policies. A bad release stops meaning a two-day review wait.

benefits.title: Native where it earns it
benefits.description: Where the framework ends, we write Swift and Kotlin: payments, camera, Bluetooth, background tasks. Planned as native modules up front, not discovered in month three.

approach.title: Scope the native boundary
approach.description: Before estimating anything we list every feature that needs native code: sensors, payments, background work. That list decides the architecture and makes the estimate honest.

approach.title: Upgrades as routine, not crisis
approach.description: We keep the app within one release of React Native stable, budget the upgrade work explicitly, and leave you a maintenance plan with real numbers instead of a surprise.

CI/CD pipeline with automated delivery to both stores

faq.q: Is React Native fast enough for our app?
faq.a: For most business apps, yes: the new architecture runs on JSI with the Hermes engine, and lists, forms and dashboards are indistinguishable from native for users. The honest exceptions are heavy real-time graphics, video processing and games. If your app lives there, we will say so and point you to Flutter or native instead.

faq.q: How much code is actually shared between iOS and Android?
faq.a: In the apps we ship, 85 to 95 percent. The rest is native modules, platform configuration and small per-platform UI adjustments. The share drops when an app leans heavily on platform hardware, which is exactly what we scope before you commit.

faq.q: What does maintenance really cost?
faq.a: Plan for a React Native and dependency upgrade cycle two or three times a year, a few engineer-days each when done on schedule. Skipping upgrades for a year turns those days into weeks, so our maintenance plans keep the cadence. Expo has cut this cost significantly in recent years.

faq.q: React Native or Flutter?
faq.a: If you have a React web team or share logic with a web product, React Native leverages what you already own. If your product is design-led with heavy custom UI and animation, Flutter's own renderer is the better fit. We build both, and the recommendation you get is written down with reasons.

flutter.label: Technologies
flutter.title: Flutter
flutter.subtitle: Your design, rendered pixel for pixel on iOS and Android from one Dart codebase. Built for products where the interface is the product.
overview: Flutter ships iOS and Android from a single Dart codebase, but its real difference is how it draws: the framework renders every pixel itself through the Impeller engine instead of mapping to platform widgets. Your interface looks and behaves identically on a three-year-old Android phone and the latest iPhone, and one team maintains one backlog for both stores.

It wins when the interface is the product: brand-heavy consumer apps, animation-rich experiences, custom design systems that would be expensive to build twice. Because Flutter compiles Dart to native machine code and controls the whole render pipeline, performance is predictable, and 60 or 120 frames per second is an engineering budget, not a hope. The same codebase reaches desktop and embedded targets when that matters.

The trade-offs are real and we name them. Dart is a separate skill, so an existing React web team carries over less than with React Native. Apps ship larger than native ones, platform-specific features go through platform channels into Swift and Kotlin, and a platform-conventional look takes deliberate work. We tell you before the project, not during it, whether those costs are worth what Flutter buys you.

benefits.title: Design survives both platforms
benefits.description: Flutter draws the interface itself, so the product ships as designed: no per-platform drift, no OEM widget surprises, one visual QA pass instead of two.

benefits.title: Performance as a budget, not a hope
benefits.description: Dart compiles ahead of time to machine code and Impeller renders without shader jank. We set frame-time and startup budgets in CI and hold them.

benefits.title: One team, one backlog
benefits.description: Typical products share well over 90 percent of code between platforms. Features land in both stores the same day, and a bug is fixed once.

benefits.title: Room to grow beyond phones
benefits.description: The same codebase targets desktop and embedded screens. If a kiosk, tablet or in-car surface is on your roadmap, Flutter reaches it without a rewrite.

approach.title: Prove the hardest screen first
approach.description: We build your riskiest interface, the signature animation or the dense dashboard, as a spike in the first days. The economics of the whole project rest on it, so it goes first.

approach.title: Design system as code
approach.description: Your brand tokens, typography and components become a Flutter package with a live gallery. Designers review real rendered widgets, not approximations.

approach.title: Vertical slices to both stores
approach.description: TestFlight and a Play internal track from the first sprints, a full slice of the product at a time. Progress is measured in installable builds.

approach.title: Measure before optimizing
approach.description: Frame times, startup and app size are tracked in CI from week one. When a number leaves its budget we fix it that sprint, not before launch.

Your design system as a documented Flutter package

faq.q: Will a Flutter app feel native?
faq.a: It feels like your product, which is exactly the point for design-led apps. Flutter ships faithful Material and Cupertino widget sets, and we adapt navigation gestures, scroll physics and haptics per platform. If your app should above all look like a stock Apple app, native or Kotlin Multiplatform is the honest recommendation.

faq.q: Is Dart hard to hire for?
faq.a: The pool is smaller than JavaScript's, but Dart is a small, typed language that an engineer coming from TypeScript, Kotlin or Swift picks up in days. Teams we hand over to routinely staff Flutter roles with strong mobile or backend engineers rather than searching for the keyword in a CV.

faq.q: Flutter or React Native?
faq.a: If your product is design-led, animation-heavy or needs identical rendering everywhere, Flutter. If you have a React web team whose code and people you want to leverage, React Native. We build both, and the recommendation you get is written down with reasons, not a preference.

faq.q: How big and fast are the apps, really?
faq.a: A minimal release build is around 10 MB per platform before assets: larger than native, but rarely decisive. At runtime it is compiled machine code with GPU rendering; on mid-range Android hardware, startup and scrolling are where Flutter routinely beats interpreted stacks. If every megabyte matters in your distribution, we will tell you what native would save.

kotlin-multiplatform.label: Technologies
kotlin-multiplatform.title: Kotlin Multiplatform
kotlin-multiplatform.subtitle: Business logic written once in Kotlin, UI kept fully native: SwiftUI on iOS, Jetpack Compose on Android. No rewrite required to start.
overview: Kotlin Multiplatform shares the code where most bugs live: networking, data models, validation, sync, business rules. Each platform keeps a fully native interface in SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose, so nothing about how the app looks or feels is compromised. Typical products end up sharing 40 to 70 percent of their code, and every shared line is written, tested and fixed once.

It wins where React Native and Flutter do not fit: you already have two native apps and teams, the platform look and feel is non-negotiable, or your domain logic is complex enough that duplicating it is your real cost. Adoption is incremental. The first shared module goes into your existing apps in weeks, no rewrite, no big-bang migration, and you can stop at any point with working software.

The honest trade-offs: you still build two user interfaces, so KMP saves less per feature than a shared-UI framework; iOS build integration adds tooling work; and the library ecosystem is younger than React Native's or Flutter's. Since JetBrains declared it stable in late 2023 and Google made it the recommended path for sharing logic, teams at Netflix, Forbes and McDonald's run it in production. We will tell you plainly whether your codebase is a fit.

benefits.title: Native UI without duplicate logic
benefits.description: SwiftUI and Compose stay exactly as your platform teams built them. What disappears is the second implementation of every business rule, API client and edge case.

benefits.title: Adopt without a rewrite
benefits.description: KMP compiles to an XCFramework your iOS app consumes like any other dependency. The first module lands in your shipping apps within weeks, and each further module is a separate decision.

benefits.title: One source of truth for the hard parts
benefits.description: Pricing rules, offline sync, validation: written once, unit-tested once, fixed once. The class of bug where iOS and Android disagree simply goes away.

benefits.title: A bet with institutional backing
benefits.description: Kotlin Multiplatform is stable, maintained by JetBrains and recommended by Google for sharing business logic. It builds on the language your Android team already writes.

approach.title: Audit the duplication
approach.description: We map both codebases and price the overlap: which logic exists twice, how often it changes, where the platforms disagree today. That is the business case, in numbers.

approach.title: Ship a real module first
approach.description: The first shared module is production code in your live apps, an API client or the sync engine, not a demo. It proves the build pipeline, the iOS interop and the team workflow at once.

approach.title: Expand along the seams
approach.description: Module by module we move domain logic into the shared core, in the order the audit ranked. Each step ships independently, and a pause always leaves a working whole.

approach.title: Make both teams owners
approach.description: iOS engineers learn to consume, then contribute to, the shared code; Android engineers learn to design APIs that feel right in Swift. We leave when the pipeline and the habits are yours.

deliverables: Shared Kotlin modules running inside your production iOS and Android apps
Architecture blueprint: what is shared, what stays native, and why
Build and publishing pipeline: XCFramework, Swift Package or CocoaPods, Maven
Test suite for the shared core, running on both platforms in CI
Sequenced migration roadmap for the remaining duplicated logic
Enablement for both platform teams: docs and hands-on sessions

faq.q: How much code can we realistically share?
faq.a: Typically 40 to 70 percent, depending on how much of your app is domain logic versus interface. That is less than React Native or Flutter promise, but it is the half where the expensive bugs live, and it comes without giving up native UI. The audit gives you the number for your codebase before you commit.

faq.q: Do our iOS developers have to write Kotlin?
faq.a: No. The shared code arrives as a standard framework with Swift-friendly APIs, and consuming it looks like using any third-party library. In practice most iOS teams start contributing to the shared module within a few months, because the alternative is waiting; that is a choice, not a requirement.

faq.q: Is Kotlin Multiplatform production-ready?
faq.a: Yes. JetBrains declared it stable in November 2023, Google recommends it for sharing logic between Android and iOS, and Netflix, Forbes, McDonald's and Cash App run it in production. The younger corner is Compose Multiplatform for shared UI; we assess that separately and recommend it only where it is ready.

faq.q: KMP, React Native or Flutter?
faq.a: Greenfield app, small team, conventional UI: React Native or Flutter usually wins on total cost. Two existing native apps, strong platform teams, complex domain logic: KMP wins, because it removes the duplication without throwing away what you built. You get the comparison for your case in writing.

items.title: Supplier invoice to posted entry
in: Supplier invoice, PDF or scan, landing in a shared mailbox
The matching purchase order and goods receipt from the ERP
Supplier master data: tax ID, bank account, payment terms

steps.title: Read
steps.desc: Pull the supplier, dates, tax ID, totals and every line item out of the document, whatever layout it arrives in.

steps.title: Match
steps.desc: Set the invoice against the order and the delivery, and mark every difference in price, quantity and VAT rate.

steps.title: Post
steps.desc: Book what agrees, attach the source file to the entry, and hand the rest over with the difference already marked.

decision.question: Do the invoice, the order and the delivery agree, and was every field read with high confidence?
decision.pass: Booked into the ERP automatically, source file attached, into the next payment run.
decision.fail: Into the accountant's queue with the difference spelled out: the order says 1,200, the invoice says 1,320.

out: A posted entry in the ERP, ready for payment
An exception queue holding only the invoices a person really needs to see
A record of every field: where on the page it was read and how sure the model was
items.human: An accountant clears the exception queue and approves anything above their limit. Nothing books itself around them.

items.title: Customer question to a sent reply
in: The incoming message, from email, chat or the contact form
Live order, delivery and invoice status out of your systems
Answers you already have: help centre, policies, resolved tickets

steps.title: Understand
steps.desc: Work out what the customer is actually asking and which order or account it concerns.

steps.title: Look up
steps.desc: Fetch the facts: where the parcel is, what was invoiced, what the policy allows in this case.

steps.title: Draft
steps.desc: Write the reply in your tone of voice, in the language the customer wrote in, with the source it used attached.

decision.question: Is this a routine case, and is every claim in the answer backed by a source?
decision.pass: Sent in seconds, ticket tagged and closed, tracking link included.
decision.fail: Handed to an agent with the draft, the facts behind it and one line on why it stopped.

out: An answer in the customer's inbox, in the language they wrote in
A ticket categorised, tagged and closed in the helpdesk
A weekly list of what people keep asking about, and where your process keeps failing them
items.human: Agents take the escalations and edit any draft they disagree with. Every edit becomes a better answer for the next customer.

items.title: Sales history to an order proposal
in: Two or three years of sales, per product and per location
Prices, promotions and the campaign calendar
Stock on hand, open orders and supplier lead times
Local context: holidays, school terms, weather

steps.title: Forecast
steps.desc: Estimate demand per product and location for next week and the next quarter, as a range rather than one number.

steps.title: Translate
steps.desc: Turn the forecast into a concrete proposal: how much to order, from which supplier, on which day.

steps.title: Track
steps.desc: Hold the forecast against what actually sold, every week, so drift shows up before it costs money.

decision.question: Does the proposal fit the buyer's limits on budget, shelf life and minimum order quantity?
decision.pass: Lands in the ERP as a draft order, ready to release in one click.
decision.fail: Goes to the buyer flagged, with the reason and the nearest proposal that does fit.

out: A ranked list of stock-out and overstock risks
Forecast against actual, tracked week by week and visible to everyone
items.human: The buyer sets the limits and keeps the last word. The system does the arithmetic across thousands of products, not the judgement calls.

items.title: Camera frame to pass or fail
in: Frames from the line camera, triggered by the controller
The reference: drawing, tolerances, an agreed set of good and bad samples
Batch, shift and machine context from the production system

steps.title: Capture
steps.desc: Photograph every part at the same angle and the same light, in step with the line.

steps.title: Compare
steps.desc: Check the part against the reference and locate the defect: a scratch, a gap, a misprint, a missing component.

steps.title: Record
steps.desc: Log the verdict with the photo, the batch and the shift, so the pattern behind the defects becomes visible.

decision.question: Is the verdict clear, or is the model unsure about this particular part?
decision.pass: A fail signal to the controller inside the cycle time. The part leaves the line and the batch record says why.
decision.fail: The photo goes to the operator's screen. Their verdict decides, and it is kept as a new example.

out: A pass or fail per part, inside the cycle time
Defect photos grouped by type, shift and machine
A growing set of examples that gets sharper with every operator verdict
items.human: Operators rule on the uncertain parts and quality sets the thresholds. The line never stops on a machine's opinion alone.

items.title: A question to a sourced answer
in: Documents where they already live: SharePoint, Drive, Confluence, network shares
Contracts, procedures, offers and technical documentation
Your existing permissions: who is allowed to see what

steps.title: Index
steps.desc: Read the documents and keep each one's permissions attached, so nothing surfaces to someone who could not open the file.

steps.title: Answer
steps.desc: Answer in the language the question was asked, quoting the passage and linking the document it came from.

steps.title: Log
steps.desc: Record every question that had no documented answer, so the gaps stop being invisible.

decision.question: Is there a documented answer, and is this person allowed to see it?
decision.pass: The answer, with a link to the exact page or clause it came from.
decision.fail: It says plainly that nothing is documented and names the person who owns that area, instead of inventing something.

out: An answer in seconds instead of asking three colleagues
Every answer traceable back to a source document
A list of the questions nobody has documented yet
items.human: The owner of each area closes the gaps the log exposes. The assistant makes them visible, it does not paper over them.

overview.title: What it is
paragraphs: The workshop is a half day of structured decision-making with senior engineers, not a seminar. We put every AI idea in your company on the table, add the ones your workflows and data suggest, and pressure-test each against two questions: what is it worth, and can it actually be built with your data and systems.

We run it remote or in your office, with the decision-maker and the people who own the problems in the room. The format is fast: map the ideas, score each on ROI and feasibility on a shared board, rank them, then pick one pilot and define what proving it would take. Everything is written down as we go.

Afterwards the debate about where to start is over. You have a shortlist your team helped rank, scores you can defend to a board, and one concrete pilot with a defined first step. Whether you build with us, in-house, or not at all, you decide from evidence instead of opinions.

overview.title: What the sprint is
paragraphs: The sprint takes one use case and answers the only question that matters before you fund a build: will this work on our data, and what will it cost in production? Senior engineers work on it full-time for two weeks, from data audit to working prototype, with a few hours a week from your domain expert.

Week one is evidence: we map your data, access, and constraints, test the risky assumptions first, and design the production architecture. Week two is the prototype: built on your real data against agreed success criteria, demoed as it grows rather than revealed at the end. You see progress midway, not just at the finish.

You end the sprint with a decision, not a feeling. Go means a prototype that already works, an architecture, and a costed roadmap the next phase executes. No-go means you saved the build budget and know exactly why: which data, constraint, or accuracy bar failed, and what would have to change.
